title: A Developer's Job Interview
subtitle: A full technical interview, from the opening question to the closing handshake.
description: A B2 reading and listening dialogue in American English: a software developer answers the five questions almost every technical interview asks, with vocabulary and comprehension exercises.
passage: Interviewer: Good morning, and thank you for coming in. Could you start by introducing yourself and telling us about your previous experience in the field?

Douglas: Good morning. My name is Douglas, and I've been working as a software developer for the past seven years. Most of my experience is in web development — JavaScript, React and Node.js — and I've also worked with databases such as MongoDB and MySQL.
Interviewer: Great. Can you give us an example of a project you worked on that you're particularly proud of?

Douglas: Sure. I was responsible for building a web application that let patients book appointments with their doctors. I used React on the front end and Node.js on the back end. The application had to handle a lot of traffic, so I had to optimize the code to make sure it stayed fast as it scaled. I also integrated it with a payment gateway so that users could pay for their appointments online.
Interviewer: That sounds impressive. Can you tell us about a challenging technical problem you faced, and how you solved it?

Douglas: One of the hardest problems I've run into involved real-time data streaming. The data was arriving at a very high rate and we needed to process it as it came in, not overnight. I used Apache Kafka and Apache Spark to handle the stream and process it efficiently. It took a while to get right, but the solution met the requirements the client had set.
Interviewer: Excellent. How do you keep yourself up to date with the latest trends and technologies?

Douglas: I read technical blogs, and I go to conferences and local meetups whenever I can. I'm active in a few online communities where developers share what they've learned. I also experiment on my own — I build small side projects with anything new, because reading about a tool and actually using it are two different things.
Interviewer: Finally, could you tell us about your experience working in a team?

Douglas: I've worked in both small and large teams. I think communication is the thing that decides whether a team works, so I try to communicate clearly and often, and I'd rather over-share than let someone find out too late. I like collaborating, and I'm always willing to help a colleague who's stuck. In my last two jobs we used Git and Jira to manage and track our work, and I'm comfortable with agile methods like Scrum.
Interviewer: Thank you for your time, and for sharing your experience with us. We'll be in touch soon.

exercises.title: Understanding the Interview
exercises.instructions: These questions ask what the candidate is demonstrating, not only what he says.

items.prompt: What does Douglas emphasize when he describes the booking application?
options: That the design won an award
That he built it alone, without any help
That it had to keep performing under heavy use, which shaped how he wrote it
items.explanation: He says the application “had to handle a lot of traffic, so I had to optimize the code to make sure it stayed fast as it scaled” — the constraint is the point of the story.

items.prompt: Why was the streaming project difficult?
options: The data arrived faster than a normal overnight process could absorb, so it had to be handled as it came in
The data was stored in an unfamiliar format
The client kept changing the requirements
items.explanation: “The data was arriving at a very high rate and we needed to process it as it came in, not overnight.”

items.prompt: Douglas names Kafka and Spark. What is he showing the interviewer by doing so?
options: That he prefers open-source tools on principle
That he chose tools suited to the specific problem, rather than listing technologies at random
That he had used those tools at university
items.explanation: The tools appear as the answer to a stated problem — high-rate, real-time data — which is what makes the example convincing rather than decorative.

items.prompt: Why does Douglas build side projects?
options: To earn extra income outside his job
Because he believes reading about a technology is not the same as having used it
items.explanation: “Reading about a tool and actually using it are two different things.”

items.prompt: What is Douglas's stated view of communication in a team?
options: That it decides whether the team works at all, so he would rather say too much than too little
That it matters less than technical skill
That it should be kept to scheduled meetings
items.explanation: “Communication is the thing that decides whether a team works… I'd rather over-share than let someone find out too late.”

items.prompt: The interviewer's questions move from experience, to a proud project, to a hard problem, to learning, to teamwork. Why that order?
options: It follows the order of the candidate's résumé
It moves from background, through evidence of ability under pressure, to how he would fit the team
It is random; interviewers ask whatever comes to mind
items.explanation: Each question tests something the previous one cannot: what he has done, what he can do when it is hard, whether he keeps growing, and whether others can work with him.

items.prompt: What does “We'll be in touch soon” tell the candidate about the outcome?
options: Nothing definite — it is the standard polite close, and the decision has not been shared
That he has been offered the job
items.explanation: It is a fixed courtesy formula at the end of an interview. It promises contact, not a result.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches what Douglas actually says.

items.statement: Douglas has worked with more than one kind of database.
items.explanation: True — he names MongoDB and MySQL.

items.statement: The booking application handled payments outside the system, by cash or bank transfer.
items.explanation: False — he integrated a payment gateway “so that users could pay for their appointments online”.

items.statement: Douglas says the streaming problem was solved quickly and easily.
items.explanation: False — “it took a while to get right”.

items.statement: He relies only on formal training to stay current.
items.explanation: False — blogs, conferences, meetups, online communities and his own side projects are all informal.

items.statement: He has experience of teams of different sizes.
items.explanation: True — “I've worked in both small and large teams.”

items.statement: Scrum is described as a tool for tracking tasks.
items.explanation: False — Git and Jira are the tools; Scrum is named as an agile method, a way of working.

exercises.title: Interview Language
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the expression that fits. These are phrases you would use in your own interview.

items.prompt: The site slowed down badly under load, so we had to ___ the database queries.
items.explanation: To optimize is to change something so it runs faster or uses fewer resources.

items.prompt: The hardest problem I've ___ ___ was a memory leak that only appeared in production.
items.explanation: To run into a problem is to meet one you did not expect.

items.prompt: I go to local ___ to hear what other developers are building.
items.explanation: A meetup is an informal local gathering of people in the same field.

items.prompt: The system has to ___ to a hundred thousand users without rewriting it.
items.explanation: To scale is to keep working well as demand grows.

items.prompt: I build small ___ projects in my own time to try out new tools.
items.explanation: A side project is something you build outside your paid work.

items.prompt: Thank you for coming in — we'll be ___ ___ by the end of the week.
items.explanation: To be in touch is to make contact. It is the standard close to an interview.

discussion: Which of the five questions would you find hardest to answer about your own work? Why?
Douglas answers the teamwork question by talking about communication rather than technical skill. Was that a good choice?
How do you keep up with developments in your own field?
Some companies replace the interview with a practical task. Which would show your ability better, and why?

Answer this in about 100 words, as you would in the interview: “Tell us about a challenging problem you faced and how you solved it.” Name the problem, say why it was hard, say what you did, and end with the result — the same four steps Douglas uses.
